definition.text: Combining trees, forage plants and grazing livestock on the same land so each benefits the others.

facts.text: It is a form of agroforestry that uses managed grazing.
Selling tree crops, forage and livestock together can raise productivity and long-term income.
Partial tree cover moderates temperature: one study found near-ground air up to 7% cooler than in open pasture.
Carbon uptake is lowest in open pastures, intermediate in silvopastures and highest in forests.
It needs heavy upfront investment and typically takes 3–6 years to give returns.
Barriers include policy hurdles, land tenure, lack of knowledge, economic constraints and cultural change.
If done correctly it can count as a nature-based solution to climate change.

definition.text: A traditional European system in which open woodland gave grazing animals shelter and forage while also yielding timber and fuel.

facts.text: It is one of the oldest land-use practices in human history.
Since Roman times, pigs have been turned into beech and oak woods to eat acorns and beech mast.

definition.text: An economic approach that aims to renew capital assets, treating the Earth as the original capital asset, instead of using them up.

facts.text: In standard theory an asset can be regenerated or consumed until it no longer yields goods or services.
Supporters say ignoring nature's value has caused uneconomic growth, Herman Daly's term, which they see as its opposite.
It has four components: circulation, organisational structure, relationships and values, and collective learning.
Unlike ecological economics, which sets limits on the economy, it focuses on the reproduction of life in nature.

definition.text: Investing that builds on sustainable finance to support ecological health, social well-being and economic resilience.

facts.text: It often, but not only, uses decentralized finance.

definition.text: Contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming.

facts.text: It comes from single discharge points and, more often, from diffuse non-point sources across the landscape, as well as air pollution.
Farm pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts, reaching lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater.
Runoff concentrated in large water bodies causes dead zones downstream.
Poor management, such as overgrazing, ploughing and badly timed pesticide use, drives much of it.
Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on pollutants entering the environment.
Agricultural economists design incentives to control such externalities, for example water pollution from farming.

definition.text: The loss of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized fields into water and air, where they cause pollution.

facts.text: Fertilizers vastly raised yields: at 1900 yield levels, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land.
Nitrate dissolves easily, so it runs off into surface water and leaches into groundwater.
Nitrate above 10 mg/L in groundwater can cause blue baby syndrome in infants.
Phosphorus is the largest contributor to eutrophication, especially in fresh water.
Fertilization also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that harms stratospheric ozone.

definition.text: The tendency of some pesticides to stay in the environment for many years after use.

facts.text: Without pest control, crop losses before harvest would typically reach 40 percent.
2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years; DDT and dieldrin are also long-lived.

title: Agricultural plastic pollution
article: Agricultural pollution#From equipment and agricultural plastics

definition.text: Plastic from greenhouse sheeting, storage bags, silage wrap and mulch film that ends up in farmed land.

facts.text: A 2021 FAO study estimated farming produces 10 million tons of plastic waste a year.
Very little agricultural plastic is collected worldwide.

title: Livestock greenhouse gas estimates
article: Agricultural pollution#Greenhouse gases from fecal waste

definition.text: The dispute over how large a share of human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock.

facts.text: The FAO estimated 18% of human greenhouse gases come directly or indirectly from livestock, more than transport.
Critics say the comparison is unfair because the FAO used a full life-cycle assessment for livestock but not for transport.
Others claim livestock could cause up to 51% of emissions.

contested_note: Estimates of livestock's share of emissions range from 18% to up to 51%, and the FAO method has been called a misrepresentation.

conflicts.text: The global livestock industry could be responsible for up to 51% of greenhouse gases.
conflicts.note: Contrasts with the FAO estimate of 18% (c72927210c59); the two rest on different accounting choices.

title: Biological pest control risks

definition.text: The debate over releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to control farm pests in place of pesticides.

facts.text: Biocontrol can cut pollution from pesticide use.
Once released, an agent may be impossible to recall and may spread into the wild or switch to native hosts.

contested_note: The merits of introducing non-native biocontrol agents are widely debated.

definition.text: Handling and treating animal waste to limit air, soil and water pollution.

facts.text: The EPA suggests one dairy farm with 2,500 cows makes as much waste as a city of around 411,000 people.
Treatment reduces the manure to transport, nutrients to spread and pathogens.
Anaerobic digestion breaks down liquid manure without air, producing fertilizer liquid and methane that can be burned for heat and power.
